extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical mechanics/statics (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of fundamental principles governing static equilibrium (virtual work, Maupertuis, Lagrange, classification of equilibria) with geometric/physical illustrations and methodological commentary on how such principles are established and accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of virtual displacements (equilibrium condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The general expression of the condition of equilibrium is that the sum of the virtual moments (projections of infinitely small mutually compatible displacements in the directions of the forces) is equal to zero; when displacements are not all reversible the sum is equal to or less than zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projections of virtual displacements in directions of the forces are taken positive. If for every virtual displacement there exists an equal and opposite one (reversible case, e.g., simple machines), one may restrict to equality (sum = 0). If some displacements cannot be reversed (strings, contacts, limits of motion), then possible rises of the centre of gravity without the converse imply the more general inequality (sum ≤ 0). Examples: replacing forces by strings over pulleys to visualize the work; positive projection convention; pay attention to reversibility of constraints when applying the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange's pulley reduction (deduction of the principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lagrange's deduction replaces all forces by an equivalent single weight Q/2 by arranging ideal pulleys so that each original force is represented by an integer number of turns of a string bearing the weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction renders the action of a single weight more immediate to experience and makes the similarity of simple and complicated cases palpable. Caution: the Lagrangian deduction presupposes the notion of work (the replacement of forces by a single weight that does the same work assumes understanding of work) and therefore does not constitute a proof that work is the determinative factor of disturbance of equilibrium — it is more an expedient/illustration than a foundational proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreversible constraints and inequality form of equilibrium condition
rubrics_metrics.description: When displacements are not all reversible (e.g., bodies connected by strings that can approach but not recede, contacts that prevent penetration), there exist displacements for which the centre of gravity may rise while the converse displacements are impossible; therefore the condition of equilibrium must be stated as the sum of the virtual moments being equal to or less than zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize physical constraints (one-way motions, non-penetration) and use the inequality form (≤ 0) rather than the strict equality. Examples: strings limiting separation, sliding/rolling where separation is permitted but penetration is not; these cases change stability considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maupertuis' principle (Loi de repos): extremum of work at equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: Maupertuis observed that the work done in passing from a given initial configuration to a final configuration which is a configuration of equilibrium is generally a maximum or a minimum; i.e., at an equilibrium configuration the differential (variation) of the work is equal to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation via the Lagrange-pulley picture: the descent/upward motion of the representative weight Q/2 as the system is displaced gives a graphical sense of whether the equilibrium corresponds to a maximum or minimum of the work. Use this to determine whether small displacements will be continued or reversed (stability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of equilibria (stable, unstable, mixed, neutral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stable equilibrium corresponds to the lowest position of the representative weight (or to a maximum of work in the system); unstable equilibrium corresponds to the highest position (or to a minimum of work); mixed equilibrium occurs at a point of contrary flexure (stable for some disturbances, unstable for others); neutral (indifferent) equilibrium occurs when small displacements neither continue nor reverse (flat locus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphical cues: pencil tracing the locus of Q/2 — a local minimum/maximum, cusp pointing up/down, or horizontal finite segment indicate the type. Examples: heavy homogeneous triaxial ellipsoid on different axes (smallest axis → stable; longest → unstable; mean → mixed); sphere or right cylinder for indifferent equilibrium; cube rolling example in figure. Note: some equilibria do not correspond to extrema (mixed/neutral), and mixed equilibrium may be regarded as unstable by some authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical representation via locus/surface of the representative weight Q/2
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the forces by Lagrange pulleys and follow the position of the single representative weight Q/2 as the system is displaced; the curve (or surface) traced by Q/2 is a convenient visual symbol of the phenomena of work and equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each point is constrained to a curve and one point determines others, Q/2 describes a curve; if points move on surfaces, Q/2 describes a surface; in higher degrees of freedom the locus still serves as a helpful symbolic representation. Use the pencil-on-paper horizontal-sheet device to see adjacent configurations and determine whether the weight tends to descend (instability) or ascend (stability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Path independence of work for forces depending only on configuration (conservative behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the forces depend on the positions of the points of the system (but not on time) the depth of descent of the representative weight Q/2 is in every case the measure of the work performed; this work is always the same for the same configuration and is independent of the path of transference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forces that vary with displacement can be realized by contrivances (e.g., a wheel and axle with non-circular wheel) so that a constant weight produces a varying force. Still, the work between two configurations is a function only of those configurations (conservative case). This justifies the energetic/comparative arguments used in Maupertuis’ principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtivron relation between work extremum and vis viva
rubrics_metrics.description: If at a configuration of equilibrium the work done is a minimum, the vis viva (kinetic energy) of the system in motion through that configuration is also a minimum (and conversely for maxima).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This links statical extremum principles (work) with dynamical quantities (vis viva). Use when relating equilibrium configurations to properties of motion through those configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium criterion via lowest centre of gravity (physical intuition for chain/catenary)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a system of connected heavy bodies (e.g., a freely suspended chain fixed at both ends), equilibrium corresponds to the configuration at which the system's centre of gravity is as low as possible — when none of the masses can sink lower without raising an equivalent mass elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a direct physical criterion for finding equilibrium shapes (e.g., catenary problem). Reduce the problem to a mathematical extremum problem: find the curve minimizing the centre of gravity for a fixed length and end positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and acceptance of principles: empirical grounding and methodological caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles (like virtual displacements) are primarily the ascertainment and establishment of facts observed in nature; their acceptance should rest on repeated application, comparison with experience, and frequent testing rather than on convoluted deductive proofs alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early discoverers should seek out cardinal facts; later workers may organize and deduce consequences. After reasonable testing, it is science to accept a principle without further derivation from other observations of the same character. Avoid overvaluing purely formal demonstrations that do not add empirical substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warnings about 'mania for demonstration' and limits of deductive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency to demand demonstrations everywhere leads to a false and mistaken rigor: some propositions are erroneously held to be more certain because they are deduced rather than observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake derivations founded on the same kind of observational evidence for a higher degree of certainty. Historical derivations (e.g., some of Archimedes' or Daniel Bernoulli's) may display this erroneous rigor; prefer clarity about the empirical basis of principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinctive knowledge versus deliberate observed principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinctive knowledge (intuitive/generalised experiences) enjoys exceptional confidence but is itself experimental and liable to error; it should ultimately yield to clearly and deliberately observed and tested principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that instinctive generalisations (taken as a priori) are useful but must be critically examined and, where necessary, replaced or refined by systematic observation and testing when new regions of experience are encountered.
